paragraphs.text: Sound is to the ocean what light is to the air. Water absorbs light within a few tens of metres and carries sound for hundreds of kilometres, so an animal that lives there and needs to find food, a mate or its own young will use sound to do it. Every group of marine mammals has arrived at the same solution independently, and the variety of what they produce is far wider than the word song suggests. Clicks, moans, pulses and whistles all do different work, and the animals that use them are not closely related to one another.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The recordings that began the field were made by accident. Military hydrophones installed to listen for submarines picked up long, repeating patterns that nobody could explain, and a small number of biologists were eventually allowed to analyse them. What they found was a sequence of units, arranged into phrases and themes, repeated for hours with the structure preserved, and the description that followed used the vocabulary of music because no other vocabulary fitted the data. The choice of words has caused trouble ever since, because a word borrowed from music carries expectations that the animals never agreed to.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Humpback song has a property that still surprises people who meet it for the first time: it changes, and every singer in an ocean basin changes with it. A new variation introduced by a few animals spreads through the population within a season or two, and the old version is abandoned rather than retained alongside. Changes have been tracked moving from one side of an ocean to the other over several years, which makes the song one of the few documented cases of cultural transmission at that scale outside our own species.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Sperm whales work differently and are in some ways more interesting. Their sound is a pattern of clicks, and groups share a distinctive rhythm that identifies them to other groups; animals with the same pattern associate and share care of calves, while animals with a different pattern living in the same water do not. The pattern is learned rather than inherited, which means the ocean contains populations that overlap physically and behave as separate communities. Two animals of the same species in the same water may have nothing to do with one another for their whole lives.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: What none of this establishes is language. The units are structured and are combined according to rules, but nobody has shown that a particular sequence refers to a particular thing, which is the property that separates language from an elaborate signal. Researchers in the field are notably careful here, and the caution is not false modesty: the same recordings are used by popular accounts to claim far more than the data supports, and the claims come back as disappointment when they are not confirmed.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Noise is the applied problem. Shipping has raised background sound in the frequencies these animals use by a large factor over a century, and a whale that must call more loudly, more often or not at all loses range that cannot be replaced. The effect is measurable in behaviour and in stress hormones, and it was demonstrated unusually clearly when shipping stopped for several weeks after a maritime incident and the recorded background fell while measured stress in nearby animals fell with it.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: The remedies are known and are mostly about ships rather than about whales. A vessel that slows by a few knots is substantially quieter, propellers designed to avoid cavitation are quieter still, and routing traffic away from feeding grounds removes the problem rather than reducing it. None of these requires new science, all of them cost something, and the ports that have tried voluntary schemes report that a discount on harbour dues achieves more than an appeal to conservation.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The field is now producing more data than it can analyse. Autonomous recorders left on the sea floor for a year return terabytes, and automatic detection of calls is improving quickly, which raises a familiar problem: a model trained on the calls of one population may not recognise the calls of another, and the calls change. What the recorders have already shown is that the ocean is noisier, more populated and more structured than the first hydrophone operators imagined when they were listening for something else entirely.
paragraphs.label: H

paragraphs.text: A canal is a river that has been argued into a straight line, and the argument is mostly with gravity. Water finds a level, so a channel dug across a landscape will run only as far as the land is flat; to carry a boat up a hill, the builder must either follow the contour for a long way, cut a deep trench, or raise the water in steps. The lock, which does the last of these, is the invention that made the canal a general technology rather than a local one. Before it, a waterway went where the valley allowed; after it, a waterway went where the money was.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The principle is stated in a sentence and takes a season to build. A chamber with gates at both ends is filled or emptied to match the level on either side; a boat enters at one level, the gates close, the water is let in or out through openings in the gates or the walls, and the boat leaves at the other. No pumps are needed, because the water comes from the upper reach by gravity, and every use of a lock sends a chamber-full of water downhill, which is the fact that decides where canals can be built.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Water supply is therefore the real constraint on a canal, not earth-moving. A busy flight of locks can consume a large volume in a day, and a summit reach that runs out of water stops the traffic on both sides of it. Builders solved this with reservoirs on the hills above, with back-pumping where fuel was cheap, and with side ponds that catch half the water from a lock and return it to the next filling. The engineering that survives is mostly about water rather than about boats. A visitor looking at a flight of locks is usually looking at a water-management scheme with a towpath beside it.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Where a hill is too steep for locks, other machines were tried. Inclined planes carried boats up a slope in a cradle on rails, either floating in a tank of water or resting on their own hulls; boat lifts raised whole chambers vertically, counterbalanced against a second chamber or against weights. Several of these are still working, one of them for more than a century, and they are faster than a flight of locks and far more expensive to maintain, which is why they are rare rather than because they did not work.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: The canal age was short and its effects were long. In the decades before railways, canals moved coal, stone, grain and pottery at a cost per tonne that roads could not approach, and the industries that grew up along them stayed after the traffic left. Railways took the freight within a generation of arriving, and most canal companies were bought by railway companies, often specifically in order to close them, which is one of the less edifying episodes in the history of transport regulation.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: What saved many canals was that filling them in cost more than leaving them. Abandoned channels remained as drainage, as water supply for industry and as an obstacle nobody had a budget to remove, and they were still there when the use that now dominates arrived. Restoration for leisure began with volunteers clearing weed at weekends, and several derelict routes reopened as through waterways because a few hundred people spent twenty years on them.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Modern canals do something different and are enormous. Ship canals carry ocean vessels between seas, their locks are measured in hundreds of metres, and the water they use per transit is such that the largest of them recycle it through basins beside the chambers. They have the same constraint as a narrow canal in a hill country, expressed in different units: what limits a ship canal is not the size of the gates but whether there is enough water at the summit in a dry year.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The lesson that engineers draw from the old canals is about maintenance rather than construction. A canal is a long thin structure that leaks, silts and grows weed, and it fails at the weakest of thousands of points; the ones that survive are those that were repaired continuously by somebody whose job it was. Several restored routes have closed again within a decade for exactly this reason, which is a warning that applies well beyond waterways.
paragraphs.label: H

paragraphs.text: A patent is a bargain with an unusual shape: an inventor is given the right to stop others using an idea for twenty years, and in exchange publishes how it works. The purpose is stated in the oldest patent laws and has not changed — to encourage invention by making it profitable, and to spread knowledge by making it public. Whether the bargain delivers either half is an empirical question, and the evidence is messier than the confidence of either side in the argument.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Elena Kovač defends the system on the ground that some inventions are expensive to make and cheap to copy. A new medicine costs a great deal to develop and can be reproduced by a competent chemist for very little, and without a period of exclusivity nobody would fund the development. She notes that the industries where this asymmetry is largest are precisely the industries where patents are most used and most valued, and she regards that correlation as the central evidence in the system’s favour.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Rahul Varma agrees about medicines and doubts the generalisation. In most manufacturing, he argues, the advantage of being first, the cost of retooling a factory and ordinary trade secrecy protect an inventor perfectly well, and surveys of firms find that patents come well down the list of reasons for investing in research in every sector except pharmaceuticals and chemicals. The system, he suggests, is defended with the example where it works and applied in the many where it does not.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Mei-Ling Choi studies what happens when patents multiply. In fields where a product touches thousands of patents — a telephone, a piece of software — the cost of finding out what one may lawfully build can exceed the cost of building it, and firms accumulate portfolios mainly to threaten each other rather than to protect a specific invention. Her studies of litigation find that in such fields a large share of suits are brought by companies that make nothing at all, which is a use of the system that its designers did not imagine.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Tomas Reinhardt is interested in the second half of the bargain, which is disclosure. The requirement to publish was supposed to let others learn from an invention, and in principle it does; in practice, he argues, many modern specifications are written to satisfy an examiner while telling a reader as little as possible, and engineers in several industries report that they do not read patents at all, partly because of that and partly because knowingly infringing a patent carries heavier penalties than infringing one you had not read.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: The historical evidence is genuinely mixed and both sides quote it. Countries that abolished or never had patents during the nineteenth century continued to innovate, sometimes conspicuously, which is used to argue that the system is unnecessary; the same countries adopted patents later, often under pressure from trading partners, which is used to argue that the earlier record was a special case. Studies of particular technologies find that patents sped up disclosure and slowed down improvement, which is the same finding described twice.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Reform proposals are narrower than the argument suggests and are mostly technical. Shorter terms for fast-moving fields, higher fees for renewal so that unused patents lapse, stricter tests of whether an invention is genuinely new, better-funded examiners with more time per application, and specialist courts to reduce the value of filing a weak suit in a friendly jurisdiction: none of these is radical, most have been tried somewhere, and the evidence for them is stronger than the evidence for either abolition or expansion.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The reasonable conclusion is that the question is badly posed. Patents are not one institution but a family of arrangements that behave differently in a laboratory, a factory and a software company, and asking whether they help invention is like asking whether contracts help business. The useful questions are narrower: in which fields, at what length, with what quality of examination, and at whose expense. Those questions have answers, and the answers vary, which is why the general argument has run for two centuries without moving. A debate that ignores the differences between fields will keep producing the same two speeches, and the two speeches have not persuaded anybody for a very long time.
paragraphs.label: H

groups.instruction: Look at the following statements and the list of people below. Match each statement with the correct person, A–D.

items.quote: and in exchange publishes how it works
items.prompt: What is the second half of the patent bargain?

options.text: A fee paid to the state.
Publication of how the invention works.
A limit on the price charged.

explanation.en: “in exchange publishes how it works” → B.
explanation.kk: «in exchange publishes how it works» → B.
explanation.ru: «in exchange publishes how it works» → B.

items.quote: the cost of finding out what one may lawfully build can exceed the cost of building it
items.prompt: What does Choi say about crowded fields?

options.text: Finding out what may lawfully be built can cost more than building it.

explanation.en: “can exceed the cost of building it” → B.
explanation.kk: «can exceed the cost of building it» → B.
explanation.ru: «can exceed the cost of building it» → B.

items.quote: Studies of particular technologies find that patents sped up disclosure and slowed down improvement
items.prompt: How does the writer describe studies of particular technologies?

options.text: They find faster disclosure and slower improvement.
They are too few to matter.

explanation.en: “sped up disclosure and slowed down improvement” → B.
explanation.kk: «sped up disclosure and slowed down improvement» → B: бір байқау екі жақтан айтылған.
explanation.ru: «sped up disclosure and slowed down improvement» → B: это одно наблюдение с двух сторон.

items.quote: The reasonable conclusion is that the question is badly posed.
items.prompt: What is the writer’s conclusion?

options.text: Patents should be abolished in most fields.
The general question is badly posed and the useful questions are narrower.
The system works as its designers intended.

explanation.en: “the question is badly posed”, followed by the narrower questions → B.
explanation.kk: «the question is badly posed» және одан кейінгі нақты сұрақтар → B.
explanation.ru: «the question is badly posed» и далее список узких вопросов → B.
